I ran a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for the hydrogen molecule H2. The bond length was 0.735 angstrom and the model was the minimal STO-3G basis. A standard mapping reduces this problem to a 2-qubit energy formula. The formula is E = -1.05237 + 0.39794 Z0 - 0.39794 Z1 - 0.01128 Z0Z1 + 0.18093 X0X1, plus a nuclear repulsion of 0.71997 hartree. All energies below are total energies in hartree.

The circuit has one adjustable angle, theta. It builds a mix of two electron arrangements. Theta sets how much of each arrangement goes into the mix. A local simulator ran the variational loop. It first tried 73 angles from -pi to pi and then narrowed in on the best one. For example, theta = 0.35 gave +0.489, theta = 2.44 gave -0.814, and theta = pi gave -1.117, which is the simple Hartree-Fock answer. The best angle was theta = -2.918. At that angle a perfect quantum computer gives -1.13730604 hartree. Solving the 4x4 energy matrix exactly also gives -1.13730604 hartree, which is the known full CI value. The variational answer matches the exact answer to about 1e-15 hartree. That is far inside chemical accuracy, which is 0.0016 hartree.

Next I sent the best circuit to garnet:mock as one job with 2 circuits and 1000 shots each. The job ID is 01a1603f-a9cb-7550-9d7a-e1ae89a1778c. The first circuit measures the Z terms. The second circuit rotates both qubits first and then measures the X0X1 term. The job completed and cost 0 credits. The mock is a free test device and returns random bitstrings that do not depend on the circuit. It returned 00 and 11 in about equal numbers for both circuits. Those counts give -0.1628 hartree, which is about 0.97 hartree above the true value. The large gap is caused by the mock device. It is not a flaw in the method. A perfect device would give mostly 10 in the Z circuit (98.8 percent) and a 19/31/31/19 percent split in the X circuit, which yields -1.1373. A real QPU would land near that value but somewhat higher, because gate and readout noise raise the measured energy.

The principle is the variational principle. Every circuit setting gives an energy that is equal to or higher than the true lowest energy. So a classical computer can keep adjusting the circuit, the quantum computer measures the energy for each setting, and the lowest value found is the best estimate of the ground state energy. The scripts are /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-12/vqe_h2.py and /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-12/h2_circuits.json. The raw result is in /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-12/h2_result.json.
